name: milking charms

attributes.attribute: rituals to protect the milk supply of a family
most needed at Beltane and Lughnasa
used rowan twigs, wax, juniper, hair balls, and metal pins

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Milking charms were rituals meant to protect a family's milk supply. Celtic people lived much on cattle food, so they made many superstitions to guard their milk, butter, and cheese. A herder let the first drops of milk splatter on the ground. He made the sign of the cross over the cow's udder and spoke charms and prayers. There were also taboos. No one could step in spilled milk or cross in front of a cow that had kicked over a pail. At Beltane, the May Day start of summer, the charms were most needed. Fairies and witches roamed about, trying to steal the milk from the cows' udders. People tied twigs of rowan to the cows' tails and rubbed melted candle wax into their hides. In Scotland the charms went with Lughnasa, the harvest feast of August 1. Folks burned juniper before the barn, sprinkled stale urine on the door, or put balls of hair in the milk pail. A strong charm boiled cow dung into a paste and added straight metal pins. Any witch who tried to steal milk then suffered stabbing pains until she begged mercy at the farmhouse door. Bottling urine and corking it would stop the kidneys of a thieving witch. Placing the herb pearlwort on the bull before conception protected the heifers through their milking lives.
objective: Document the milking charms of the Celtic peoples.
